Case study

A certificate can expire without changing the product

As Green Loom’s co-founder, I designed a retail catalog where a product’s lab certificate is its own record. When the certificate runs out, the store listing stops and the product stays as it was.

Role
Co-founder
Scope
Retail catalog model and operator workflow
Key decision
Keep lab evidence separate from product identity
Outcome
Selected design direction, approved wireframe baseline, and a public schema

Georgia requires a lab certificate from the last 12 months

Green Loom’s retail launch scope is Georgia consumable hemp. Georgia prohibits retail sale of hemp flower and leaves. It requires a full-panel certificate of analysis, or COA, contracted within the last 12 months and made publicly available. Product labels must show the analysis results or give direct QR access to them.

The rule puts a date on the evidence, not on the product. Nothing about a product has to change for its certificate to go out of date. As co-founder, I had to decide where that certificate lives in the catalog, and what happens to a product when its certificate runs out.

Design context: Georgia Department of Agriculture retail guidance and Georgia’s consumable-hemp rules. These sources informed the design. Hemp rules change, so check the current rules rather than this page. This case study is not a claim of legal certification.

I kept the certificate out of the product record

Early catalog concepts put product details, store listings, stock, and lab results on the same screens. They looked like fields on one product, even though they follow different rules. Potency looked editable on the product, although the lab result should be its source.

I gave the certificate its own record, a Lab Result, with its own validity period. When a certificate expires, the proposed publication check stops the store listing and names the reason. The product keeps its identity. Linking a new certificate lets the listing publish again without re-entering the product.

One model, two speeds of work

The same split runs through the rest of the catalog. Product holds shared identity and content. Variant identifies a sellable package. Listing controls how a variant is offered at a store. Inventory records quantity and availability. Lab Result holds the certificate. The interface can show these facts together without making them one record.

The interface followed the model. A guided first-publish path helps a new operator create the needed records in order. Returning operators work directly in catalog and inventory views instead of reopening a wizard for every change.

We chose this object-first approach after comparing it with a journey-led launchpad and a cross-object work queue. The tradeoff is that direct workspaces suit routine work, but the first-use path has to explain unfamiliar terms without showing every underlying record at once. The selected concept and initial wireframe baseline were approved as design direction, not as usability findings.

For technical readers

A schema for exchanged data, separate from the product model

No existing standard or vendor format gave this catalog a complete product-data contract, so Green Loom published the versioned Cannabis Product Schema. Its jurisdiction-neutral core describes Product, Package, LabResult, Label, and Party. A separate Georgia hemp profile adds local constraints without building them into the core.

The schema makes incoming and outgoing product data checkable. Retail still needs its own Product, Variant, Listing, Inventory, and Lab Result records so an operator edits the right thing. Publishing the schema is a concrete output. It is not evidence of industry adoption or legal approval.

Outcome

Approved as design direction, with operator evidence still ahead

The work produced a selected information architecture, an approved wireframe baseline, and a published schema. Later high-fidelity work is still a design candidate. An operator pilot is active. This page was written in September 2026 and does not record when the pilot started. Direct operator evidence, accessibility review, and other specialist checks are still needed before I can say the experience works in practice.

My takeaway is that simplifying a regulated workflow does not mean hiding its rules. It means keeping the right evidence authoritative and showing people why an action is available, blocked, or incomplete.

I’m glad to walk through the Green Loom model, the schema, or where the pilot stands.
